title: How first-line antitubercular drugs hit Mycobacterium tuberculosis
ariaLabel: Schematic of the tubercle bacillus: it makes mycolic acid and the arabinogalactan of its wall, makes RNA with its RNA polymerase, and keeps its membrane energy in acid conditions. Isoniazid blocks mycolic acid synthesis, ethambutol blocks arabinogalactan synthesis, rifampicin blocks RNA polymerase and pyrazinamide disturbs membrane energy in acid. The four together stop growth far more than any one alone.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Mycolic acid precursors
nodes.info: Building blocks of mycolic acids, the waxy outer layer of the mycobacterial wall.

nodes.label: Mycolic acid wall layer
nodes.info: The waxy wall layer that protects the bacillus.

nodes.label: Arabinose units
nodes.info: Sugar units for the arabinogalactan of the wall.

nodes.label: Arabinogalactan
nodes.info: A wall polysaccharide that anchors the mycolic acids.

nodes.label: Bacterial RNA and proteins
nodes.info: Without new RNA the bacillus cannot make proteins.

nodes.label: Membrane energy
nodes.info: Energy and transport of the bacillus in acidic, slow-growing conditions, as inside macrophages and in caseous foci.

nodes.label: Bacterial survival in acid
nodes.info: Slow-growing bacilli survive in acidic sites.

nodes.label: Tubercle bacilli
nodes.info: A teaching score for how well the bacilli keep growing: it falls as more of their wall, RNA and membrane energy steps are blocked.

edges.label: InhA (mycolic acid)
edges.info: Isoniazid (a prodrug activated by the bacterial KatG enzyme) blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
Adds to the bacterial growth shown at the right.

edges.label: arabinosyl transf.
edges.info: Ethambutol blocks arabinosyl transferase, so the wall's arabinogalactan is not built.
Adds to the bacterial growth shown at the right.

edges.label: RNA polymerase
edges.info: Rifampicin binds the beta subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase and stops RNA being made.
Adds to the bacterial growth shown at the right.

edges.label: membrane energy
edges.info: Pyrazinamide is converted to pyrazinoic acid, which disturbs membrane energy and transport in acid, helping to kill slow bacilli.
Adds to the bacterial growth shown at the right.

sources: Where each class acts. Isoniazid blocks mycolic acid synthesis, ethambutol blocks arabinogalactan synthesis, rifampicin blocks RNA polymerase and pyrazinamide disturbs membrane energy in acid. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Streptomycin, second-line and newer drugs, resistance and how combinations stop it, intensive and continuation phases, doses and durations, adverse effects and monitoring (hepatitis, neuropathy, optic neuritis), drug interactions and latent infection are left out. Bacterial growth is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
